name: Shilajit
lead: Shilajit (also mumijo, moumiyo or mummiyo) is a sticky, dark, tar-like substance that seeps from rock layers in high mountain ranges such as the Himalayas, long used in Ayurvedic and other traditional medicine as a rejuvenator (rasayana) and adaptogen. It consists mainly of humic substances (a review puts them at more than 80 percent of its weight) together with minerals and plant and microbial metabolites.[1][2][3]

It is sold as a resin, powder, capsule or gummy and marketed for testosterone, energy, recovery and vitality. A small randomised, placebo-controlled trial in healthy men aged 45 to 55 reported higher total testosterone, free testosterone and DHEAS after 90 days of purified shilajit.[4] Other human trials have examined bone density in postmenopausal women, fracture repair, and a collagen biomarker, while a 2024 review of testosterone boosters named a purified shilajit extract in its findings.[5][6][7][8]
Reviewers describe its chemical composition and origin as not fully established, and the human research is limited to small trials, many using proprietary purified extracts.[2]
infobox: Exudate from rock in high-altitude mountain ranges (Himalaya, Hindu Kush, Altai and others)[1][9]
Humic substances, including fulvic acid; minerals; dibenzo-alpha-pyrones[1][2][9]

paras: Shilajit is a pale-brown to blackish-brown exudate from rock layers in mountain ranges, notably the Himalayas and Hindu Kush. One review describes it as a complex mixture of organic humic substances and plant and microbial metabolites from the rock rhizosphere.[1] A 2025 review states that its exact source is uncertain: some believe it forms from dead plant residues or animal excrement, others that it is a mineral secreted from rock, and that no comprehensive chemical analysis of all its components has been performed.[2] The name comes from Sanskrit words usually glossed as 'conqueror of mountains'.[9]

Reviews of traditional Indian medicine describe shilajit as a rasayana in the Ayurvedic and Siddha systems, classified into grades associated with metals and described in classical texts.[3][9] A 2000 review of herbal exercise-performance aids lists shilajit or mummio among herbs used to enhance performance regardless of scientific evidence of effect.[10]

Traditional uses described in reviews include chronic fatigue, arthritis, diabetes, infertility and cognitive complaints.[3][9] Modern supplement marketing emphasises testosterone support, energy and performance, bone and joint health, and anti-ageing.[4][9]

In a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of healthy volunteers aged 45 to 55, 90 days of purified shilajit significantly increased total testosterone, free testosterone and DHEAS compared with placebo.[4] A 2024 systematic review of 27 testosterone boosters reported that most failed to raise total testosterone and named a purified shilajit extract (PrimaVie) in its findings alongside E. longifolia and a pomegranate-cacao blend.[5]

Other randomised trials have examined a standardised aqueous shilajit extract on oxidative stress, inflammation and bone density in 60 postmenopausal women with osteopenia;[6] momiai in tibia fracture repair;[7] an 8-week study of serum pro-collagen type I as a marker of collagen synthesis;[8] and a combination supplement with chromium and amla in people at metabolic risk undergoing diet and exercise.[11] A clinical study examined the skeletal muscle transcriptome after oral shilajit supplementation.[12]

General-reference descriptions say purified shilajit is generally well tolerated in small trials, with few reported effects such as headache, while raw forms may carry contaminants such as heavy metals, and recommend standardised, tested products; these statements are from an AI-generated encyclopedia and have not been verified here against primary sources.[9] A 2025 review notes that the chemical composition of shilajit varies by region and is not fully characterised, which has implications for product consistency.[2]

Laboratory and animal work reports antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antiulcer and immunomodulatory activity, cholinergic effects in rat brain, hepatoprotection in rats, and in vitro antiviral effects.[3][13][14][15][16] Reviews also discuss potential procognitive and Alzheimer's-related properties, based largely on preclinical data.[17][18]

Shilajit became prominent in fitness communities through podcasts and social media discussions of testosterone. T Nation members mention taking it as a gummy, as part of 'ayurvedic' stacks with ashwagandha, or as an add-on to hormone therapy, with accounts from a 'slight difference' to only 'delicate' improvement.[19][20][21]

Randomised placebo-controlled trials in humans include testosterone and DHEAS in healthy middle-aged men,[4] bone density in postmenopausal osteopenia,[6] tibia fracture repair,[7] and collagen biomarkers;[8] a clinical study of muscle gene expression;[12] and a combination-supplement trial in people at metabolic risk.[11] Registered studies include PrimaVie with exercise in obese adults (n=29) and several dietary-supplement trials of products containing shilajit.[22] Trials are small and often use proprietary extracts, and independent replication of the testosterone result is not described in the sources reviewed.

lore.intro: Shilajit is discussed on T Nation as an adaptogenic add-on to testosterone and training, sometimes via a podcaster's endorsement, with mixed personal reports.[19][20][21]

claims.believers: A T Nation post links a podcaster's discussion of shilajit for testosterone, and another poster who added it to a supplement regimen says they 'notice a slight difference'.[19][20]
claims.experts: One randomised trial in 45- to 55-year-old healthy men reported higher total and free testosterone and DHEAS versus placebo over 90 days, and a 2024 review of testosterone boosters discussed purified shilajit extract among its findings.[4][5]

claims.claim: Shilajit boosts alertness, energy and recovery
claims.believers: A T Nation post relays an acquaintance's report that taking it helped alertness after missing sleep, and posters use it alongside ashwagandha for recovery.[19][23]
claims.experts: Reviews describe adaptogenic activity from traditional use and some verified properties, but note limited controlled human data on fatigue; a 2000 review lists it among herbs used for performance regardless of evidence.[1][10]

claims.claim: Higher-altitude 'gold grade' shilajit is purer and more potent
claims.believers: Commercial descriptions say shilajit from extreme altitudes has higher fulvic acid and fewer contaminants.[9]
claims.experts: The general reference notes scientific evidence for altitude-based superiority is limited, and a 2025 review says composition varies by region and is not fully characterised.[9][2]

claims.claim: Shilajit helps bones, collagen, brain and ageing
claims.believers: Supplement marketing and traditional use cite rejuvenation and longevity.[3][9]
claims.experts: A randomised trial in postmenopausal women with osteopenia reported effects on bone-loss markers, an 8-week study measured a collagen-synthesis biomarker, and cognitive-benefit discussions rest mainly on animal and in vitro work.[6][8][17]

card.summary: Himalayan mineral resin sold for testosterone and vitality; one small trial supports a testosterone rise, and quality control is the open question.
card.note: Composition varies by source; raw resin may contain contaminants per general references, and most trials used purified proprietary extracts.

quick.overview:
Shilajit is a tar-like mountain exudate used for thousands of years in Ayurveda as a rejuvenating tonic. It is sold as a resin, capsule or gummy for testosterone, energy and recovery.

A small randomised trial in healthy men reported higher testosterone and DHEAS after 90 days of purified shilajit, and other trials have looked at bone and collagen markers. Evidence remains limited and mostly involves proprietary extracts.
quick.mechanism: It is made up mostly of humic substances such as fulvic acid plus minerals. Proposed antioxidant and hormonal effects come from lab and small human studies; its exact composition and origin are not fully characterised.
quick.risks: Purified products are described as generally well tolerated in small trials, while raw material may contain contaminants such as heavy metals according to general references. Content varies by source, and it is sold as a supplement.
